beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Surya, and this video is about LTI one point three — what actually happens in the seconds between a student clicking a tool inside Canvas and that tool knowing who they are.

show.event: title snaps in over ground, signal rule above

beats.narration_text: A student is inside Canvas, already logged in. They click your tool, which is a completely separate application on a different server. It needs to know who they are, which course they came from, and whether they are a student or an instructor — without asking them to log in a second time, and without simply believing whatever the browser tells it.

show.event: two blocks with a gap; three questions snap into the gap

beats.narration_text: None of this works on the day. Before a single launch, the two sides exchange registration details. Canvas issues a client ID and a deployment ID that identify your tool. You record Canvas's authorization endpoint and the address where it publishes its keys. Canvas records your login endpoint, your redirect endpoint, and where you publish yours. Trust is established here, in advance — not during the launch.

show.event: two registration columns fill row by row

beats.narration_text: Each side holds a private key and publishes the matching public key at a JWKS endpoint — a JSON Web Key Set. Canvas signs with its private key, and you verify with the public key you fetch from Canvas. You sign with yours, and Canvas verifies with the one you publish. Neither side ever ships the other a password. That is the whole basis of the trust.

show.event: mirrored keypairs; two arrows cross, each with its own arrowhead

beats.narration_text: The launch has four moves. Move one. Canvas calls your login endpoint and tells you which platform is calling and which user is arriving. You do not trust that yet. You generate a random state and a random nonce, store them on your own server, and redirect the browser back to Canvas's authorization endpoint, asking for an identity token.

Move two. Canvas authenticates the user itself, then posts an identity token back to your redirect endpoint. It arrives as a form post, not as a redirect with the token in the address bar, so it never lands in a browser history or a server log. The token is a JWT — a signed, self-contained statement about who this person is.

show.event: id_token posted back as a form post

beats.narration_text: Inside that token are the claims. A stable user identifier. Name and email. The role claim, saying student or instructor. The course context — its ID and title. The resource link and custom parameters, which say which piece of content they were trying to open. And the protocol fields — deployment ID, message type, version — that let you confirm the launch is the shape you were expecting.

show.event: the token's claim rows stack up, each with its purpose

beats.narration_text: Move three, and this is the one that matters. Verification is four separate checks, not one. Validate the signature against the public keys Canvas publishes. Check the issuer — that it came from the platform you registered. Check the audience — that it was meant for you. Check the expiry. And pin the algorithm to RS256, so nobody can hand you a token that asks to be trusted without a signature at all.

show.event: four checks land, then the pinned algorithm

beats.narration_text: Move four. The state and nonce you stored back at move one are checked against what came back, and consumed on read. A captured launch cannot be replayed, because the second attempt finds nothing left to match. Nonces live ten minutes. Launch records are kept for one hour, then purged.

show.event: the same launch replayed is rejected

beats.narration_text: Only now do you act on it. The role is matched against a list of official role identifiers, so a student is a student. Access is evaluated on your server on every request, never asserted by the browser. And the tool asks for no grade or roster permissions at all — so it cannot read a gradebook or a class list, because it never requested the right to.

So that is LTI one point three. Not a password shared between two systems, but two keypairs registered in advance, a signed statement passed once, verified four ways, and spent. The launch is not where the trust comes from. The registration is. The launch is just where it gets used.
